title: Transmitters & Receivers
description: Generate a stable carrier, amplify it efficiently and match it to the antenna; then receive it with a superheterodyne and work out images, sensitivity and intermodulation.

study.title: The transmitter chain
study.body: A crystal **oscillator** (XO) sets the carrier and a **buffer** isolates it from load changes. In this indirect-FM transmitter a **phase modulator** adds the audio, **frequency multipliers** (class C stages whose output tank is tuned to the 2nd or 3rd harmonic) raise carrier and deviation to the output band, and the **driver** and **power amplifier** (PA) feed the antenna through a matching network. Crystal accuracy is given in parts per million: a multiplier chain multiplies the absolute error, but the ppm value stays the same.

study.title: PLL frequency synthesizer
study.body: A phase-locked loop locks a VCO to a crystal reference: the phase detector (PD) compares $f_{ref}$ with $f_{out}/N$, and the loop filter steers the VCO until both are equal. Stepping the programmable divider $N$ by one moves the output by $f_{ref}$, so $f_{ref}$ is the **channel spacing**, and the output is as stable as the crystal. A fixed ÷$M$ prescaler (needed at high VCO frequencies) makes the step $Mf_{ref}$; a dual-modulus $M/(M+1)$ prescaler restores steps of $f_{ref}$ with a total ratio $MN + A$.

study.title: Explore: power amplifier classes
study.body: Efficiency $\eta = P_{out}/P_{DC}$; the rest heats the transistor. The less of each cycle the transistor conducts, the higher the maximum efficiency: class **A** (360°) at most 50 % (25 % with a resistive collector load), **B** push-pull (180° each) 78.5 %, **C** (< 180°, a tuned tank restores the sine) about 60–85 % in practice. Switching classes **D** and **E** approach 100 %. Only linear classes (A, AB, B) can amplify AM, SSB or QAM; class C suits FM and CW.

study.title: L-network impedance matching
study.body: One series and one shunt reactance match two resistances at one frequency. The **series** element sits on the side of the **lower** resistance, the **shunt** element across the **higher** one, and the network's $Q$ is fixed by the resistance ratio. With a series L and a shunt C (low-pass) the network also attenuates the PA harmonics. Finally $L = X_s/(2\pi f)$ and $C = 1/(2\pi f X_p)$; stray reactances are absorbed into these values.

study.title: Explore: superheterodyne and images
study.body: The mixer shifts every station to one fixed **intermediate frequency**, where fixed filters provide the selectivity. With high-side injection $f_{LO} = f_s + f_{IF}$. A signal at the **image** $f_{LO} + f_{IF} = f_s + 2f_{IF}$ (low-side: $f_s - 2f_{IF}$) produces the same IF and can only be removed by the preselector **before** the mixer. Drag $f_{IF}$ and $Q$ (receiver tuned to 100 MHz): a higher IF or a sharper preselector gives more image rejection. Dual conversion combines a high first IF (images) with a low second IF (selectivity).

study.title: Sensitivity and noise floor
study.body: Thermal noise at 290 K is $kT$ = −174 dBm in every hertz. Referred to the antenna input, a receiver with bandwidth $B$ and noise figure NF has a noise floor of −174 dBm + 10 log B + NF. Add the S/N the demodulator needs (e.g. 10 dB, or a 12 dB SINAD for FM voice) to get the **minimum detectable signal**. In a 50 Ω system 1 µV rms is −107 dBm; good receivers reach 0.2–1 µV.

study.title: Intermodulation, dynamic range, AGC and SDR
study.body: Two strong signals $f_1$, $f_2$ in a slightly nonlinear amplifier or mixer create **third-order intermodulation** products at $2f_1 - f_2$ and $2f_2 - f_1$, right next to the wanted channel where no filter can remove them; they rise 3 dB for every 1 dB of input. **Dynamic range** spans from the MDS to the largest signal handled without such distortion; **AGC** reduces the RF/IF gain on strong signals, giving 60–100 dB. In a **software-defined radio** an ADC digitizes the IF (or the RF directly) and DSP does filtering, demodulation and AGC.

steps.title: From crystal to antenna
steps.body: A transmitter builds its signal in stages. A crystal oscillator (XO) sets a stable carrier, a buffer isolates it, the modulator adds the information, frequency multipliers raise the frequency, and the driver and power amplifier (PA) bring it up to the transmit power.

steps.prompt: Put the stages of an indirect-FM transmitter in signal order.
steps.explanation: The crystal sets the carrier, the buffer protects it from load changes, the phase modulator produces a small deviation at a low frequency, and the multipliers raise **both** carrier and deviation to the output values. Driver and PA then add the power, so all the delicate work happens at low power.

steps.prompt: An oscillator with a stability of ±{{ppm}} ppm is followed by a ×{{N}} multiplier chain. The output frequency then has a stability of ±{{ppm*N}} ppm.
steps.explanation: False. The multipliers multiply the frequency **and** its absolute error by {{N}}, so their ratio, the ppm value, stays ±{{ppm}} ppm. Example: 10 MHz ± 10 Hz (1 ppm) × {{N}} = {{10*N}} MHz ± {{10*N}} Hz, still 1 ppm.

steps.title: Power amplifier classes
steps.body: The class says how much of each RF cycle the transistor conducts: **A** 360°, **B** 180° (two transistors in push-pull), **AB** a bit more than 180°, **C** less than 180° with a tuned tank that rings out a clean sine, **D/E** as a switch. Less conduction means less heat and a higher efficiency, but a class C stage loses the amplitude information.

steps.prompt: Match each amplifier class to its description.
steps.explanation: Efficiency rises as the conduction angle shrinks: A (≤ 50 %, 10–25 % typical), B (≤ 78.5 %), C (60–85 %), and the switching classes D and E, whose transistor is either fully on or fully off, approach 100 % in theory.

steps.prompt: Which signal must **not** be amplified by a class C power amplifier?
steps.explanation: A class C stage only reproduces the frequency and phase of its input; the amplitude of the output is set by the tank and supply. FM, CW and FSK have a constant envelope, so that is fine. SSB (like AM, DSB and QAM) carries information in the amplitude and needs a **linear** (class A, AB or B) amplifier.

steps.title: The superheterodyne receiver
steps.body: A tuned-radio-frequency (TRF) receiver must retune all its filters for every station, so its selectivity changes across the band. The **superheterodyne** instead mixes every station with a tunable local oscillator (LO) to one fixed **intermediate frequency** (IF), where fixed, sharp filters and most of the gain are located. With **high-side injection** the LO sits above the signal.

steps.prompt: An FM broadcast receiver with the standard 10.7 MHz IF uses high-side injection. Which LO frequency receives a station at {{fs|Hz|4}}?
steps.explanation: High-side injection: $f_{LO} = f_s + f_{IF}$ = {{fs|Hz|4}} + 10.7 MHz = **{{fs+10.7e6|Hz|4}}**. The mixer output then contains $f_{LO} - f_s$ = 10.7 MHz, which passes the IF filter.

steps.prompt: The same receiver ($f_{IF}$ = 10.7 MHz, high-side LO) is tuned to {{fs|Hz|4}}. At which frequency does a station produce **image** interference?
steps.explanation: $f_{LO}$ = {{fs+10.7e6|Hz|4}}. A signal 10.7 MHz **above** the LO also gives a 10.7 MHz difference: $f_{im} = f_s + 2f_{IF}$ = **{{fs+21.4e6|Hz|4}}**. {{fs+10.7e6|Hz|4}} is the LO itself; $f_s - 2f_{IF}$ would be the image for low-side injection.

steps.prompt: Once an image signal reaches the mixer, it lands exactly on the IF. Tap the stage whose selectivity must reject the image.
steps.explanation: Only the tuned **RF amplifier** (preselector) in front of the mixer can tell $f_s$ and $f_{im}$ apart, because they are $2f_{IF}$ apart there. After the mixer both sit on $f_{IF}$, so the IF filter, however sharp, passes the image. The IF filter provides the **adjacent-channel** selectivity instead.

steps.prompt: A {{f|Hz}} crystal oscillator is specified at ±{{ppm}} ppm. What is the largest possible frequency error?
steps.explanation: $\Delta f = f\cdot\text{ppm}\cdot 10^{-6}$ = {{f|Hz}} × {{ppm}} × $10^{-6}$ = **±{{f*ppm*1e-6|Hz}}**. The frequency lies between {{f-f*ppm*1e-6|Hz|7}} and {{f+f*ppm*1e-6|Hz|7}}.

steps.prompt: An FM transmitter uses a {{f0|Hz}} crystal oscillator (±{{ppm}} ppm) and a phase modulator that produces a deviation of {{d|Hz}}, followed by a ×{{a}} and a ×{{b}} multiplier.

ask.prompt: What is the output carrier frequency?
ask.explanation: The multiplication factors multiply: × {{a}} × {{b}} = × {{a*b}}. $f_{out}$ = {{a*b}} × {{f0|Hz}} = **{{f0*a*b|Hz}}**.

ask.prompt: What is the largest frequency error of the output carrier?
ask.explanation: The ppm value is unchanged, the absolute error is multiplied: $\Delta f$ = {{f0*a*b|Hz}} × {{ppm}} × $10^{-6}$ = **{{f0*a*b*ppm*1e-6|Hz}}** (= {{a*b}} × the oscillator's {{f0*ppm*1e-6|Hz}}).

ask.prompt: What is the frequency deviation of the output signal?
ask.explanation: A multiplier multiplies the instantaneous frequency, so the deviation grows by the same factor: {{d|Hz}} × {{a*b}} = **{{d*a*b|Hz}}**. This is why indirect FM can start with a small deviation.

steps.title: Synthesizer arithmetic
steps.body: In lock the divided VCO frequency equals the reference: $f_{out}/N = f_{ref}$. Each step of $N$ moves the output by one channel spacing $f_{ref}$. A fixed ÷$M$ prescaler in the loop multiplies both the output and the step by $M$.
steps.formula: \begin{aligned} f_{out} &= N f_{ref}\\ f_{out} &= MN f_{ref}\;\;\text{(with prescaler)}\end{aligned}

steps.prompt: A PLL synthesizer compares the divided VCO signal with a {{fr|Hz}} reference. Which divider ratio $N$ gives an output of {{N*fr|Hz|7}}?
steps.explanation: $N = f_{out}/f_{ref}$ = {{N*fr|Hz|7}} / {{fr|Hz}} = **{{N||6}}**. The next channel up needs $N$ = {{N+1||6}}: {{(N+1)*fr|Hz|7}}, one $f_{ref}$ higher.

steps.prompt: A synthesizer has a fixed ÷{{M}} prescaler between the VCO and the programmable ÷N divider, and a {{fr|Hz}} reference.

ask.prompt: What is the output frequency for $N$ = {{N}}?
ask.explanation: The total division is $MN$ = {{M}} × {{N}} = {{M*N||6}}, so $f_{out} = MNf_{ref}$ = {{M*N||6}} × {{fr|Hz}} = **{{M*N*fr|Hz|5}}**.

ask.prompt: By how much does the output frequency change when $N$ is increased by one?
ask.explanation: Each step of $N$ adds $M f_{ref}$ = {{M}} × {{fr|Hz}} = **{{M*fr|Hz}}**, not {{fr|Hz}}: the fixed prescaler coarsens the channel spacing. A dual-modulus prescaler solves this.

steps.prompt: A class C power amplifier runs from {{V|V}} and draws an average collector current of {{I|A}} while delivering {{Po|W}} to the antenna.

ask.prompt: What is its efficiency?
ask.explanation: $P_{DC} = V_{CC}I_C$ = {{V|V}} × {{I|A}} = {{V*I|W}}. $\eta = P_{out}/P_{DC}$ = {{Po|W}} / {{V*I|W}} = **{{100*Po/(V*I)|%}}**, typical for class C.

ask.prompt: How much power does the transistor dissipate?
ask.explanation: Everything not delivered to the load becomes heat: $P_D = P_{DC} - P_{out}$ = {{V*I|W}} − {{Po|W}} = **{{V*I-Po|W}}**.

steps.prompt: A linear PA must deliver {{Po|W}} at an efficiency of {{100*eta|%}}. How much heat must its heat sink remove?
steps.explanation: $P_{DC} = P_{out}/\eta$ = {{Po|W}} / {{eta}} = {{Po/eta|W}}. The dissipation is the difference: $P_D = P_{DC} - P_{out}$ = **{{Po*(1/eta-1)|W}}**. ({{Po*(1-eta)|W}} wrongly takes the losses as a fraction of the **output** power; {{Po/eta|W}} is the DC input power.)

steps.title: Designing an L network
steps.body: To match a low resistance to a higher one: compute $Q$ from the ratio, put the series reactance $X_s = QR_{low}$ next to the low resistance and the shunt reactance $X_p = R_{high}/Q$ across the high one. Here the transistor output ($R_{low}$) drives the 50 Ω antenna ($R_{high}$) through a low-pass L network.
steps.formula: \begin{aligned} Q &= \sqrt{\frac{R_{high}}{R_{low}} - 1}\\ L &= \frac{QR_{low}}{2\pi f},\quad C = \frac{Q}{2\pi f R_{high}}\end{aligned}

steps.prompt: Match the {{Rl|Ω}} output of a transistor PA to a 50 Ω antenna at {{f|Hz}} with this L network.

ask.prompt: What is the $Q$ of the network?
Find the inductance $L$.
Find the capacitance $C$.

steps.prompt: A {{Rl|Ω}} source drives a 50 Ω load through a series L and a shunt C across the load. Tune $L$ and $C$ so that the full available power reaches the load at 100 MHz.
An AM broadcast superhet with a 455 kHz IF and high-side injection is tuned to {{fs|Hz|4}}.

ask.prompt: What is the LO frequency?
What is the image frequency?

steps.prompt: A VHF receiver with a {{fif|Hz}} IF uses **low-side** injection and is tuned to {{fs|Hz|4}}.

ask.prompt: What is the LO frequency?
ask.explanation: Low-side: $f_{LO} = f_s - f_{IF}$ = {{fs|Hz|4}} − {{fif|Hz}} = **{{fs-fif|Hz|4}}**.

ask.prompt: What is the image frequency?
ask.explanation: The image is the IF on the **other** side of the LO: $f_{im} = f_{LO} - f_{IF} = f_s - 2f_{IF}$ = {{fs|Hz|4}} − {{2*fif|Hz}} = **{{fs-2*fif|Hz|4}}**.

steps.prompt: A receiver tuned to {{fs|Hz}} uses a {{fif|Hz}} IF (high-side LO) and a single tuned preselector with loaded $Q$ = {{Q}}. Its attenuation at frequency $f$ is $\sqrt{1 + Q^2\rho^2}$ with $\rho = f/f_s - f_s/f$. Find the image rejection in dB.
steps.explanation: $f_{im} = f_s + 2f_{IF}$ = {{fim|Hz|4}}. $\rho$ = {{fim/fs||4}} − {{fs/fim||4}} = {{rho||3}}, $Q\rho$ = {{Q*rho||3}}. Rejection = $20\log_{10}\sqrt{1 + (Q\rho)^2}$ = **{{10*log10(1+Q^2*rho^2)|dB}}**. A higher IF moves the image further from $f_s$ and raises this quickly.

steps.title: Noise floor in dBm
steps.body: Every receiver is limited by thermal noise $kTB$: at 290 K that is −174 dBm in 1 Hz. Widening the bandwidth 10× adds 10 dB of noise; the receiver adds its noise figure on top. The weakest usable signal is the noise floor plus the S/N the demodulator needs.

steps.prompt: A receiver has a noise bandwidth of {{B|Hz}} and a noise figure of {{NF}} dB. What is its noise floor, referred to the input?
A receiver with a {{B|Hz}} bandwidth and a {{NF}} dB noise figure needs an S/N of {{snr}} dB at the detector.

ask.prompt: What is the minimum detectable signal in dBm?
ask.explanation: Noise floor: −174 + 10 log({{B||3}}) + {{NF}} = {{P-snr||4}} dBm. Add the required S/N: $P_{min}$ = {{P-snr||4}} + {{snr}} = **{{P||4}} dBm**.

ask.prompt: Express this sensitivity as an rms voltage across the 50 Ω input.

steps.prompt: A signal generator delivers {{V|V}} rms into the 50 Ω input of a receiver. What is this power in dBm?
A two-tone test on an amplifier gives the output spectrum below (tones at 10 MHz and {{10+d}} MHz).

ask.prompt: How many dB below the tones are the third-order products?
ask.explanation: The tones are at {{Pt}} dBm, the red IM3 products (at $2f_1 - f_2$ and $2f_2 - f_1$) at {{Pt-D}} dBm: they are **{{D}} dB** below the tones (−{{D}} dBc).

ask.prompt: Both input tones are raised by 5 dB. How many dB below the tones are the third-order products now?
ask.explanation: The plot shows a gap of {{D}} dB. The tones rise 5 dB, the IM3 products 3 × 5 = 15 dB, so the gap shrinks by 10 dB: {{D}} − 10 = **{{D-10}} dB**. Third-order distortion gets worse quickly with signal level.

ask.prompt: Estimate the output third-order intercept point OIP3 = $P_{tone} + \Delta/2$, where $\Delta$ is the tone-to-IM3 difference.
ask.explanation: Tones grow 1 dB/dB, IM3 products 3 dB/dB, so the lines meet $\Delta/2$ above the tone level: OIP3 = {{Pt}} + {{D}}/2 = **{{Pt+D/2}} dBm**. A higher intercept point means a more linear stage.

steps.prompt: Match each receiver term to its meaning.
pairs: Weakest signal giving a usable output
ADC and DSP do the filtering and demodulation
steps.explanation: Sensitivity is set by noise (and gain), selectivity by the IF filter's bandwidth and shape factor. AGC lowers the gain on strong signals. SINAD includes distortion, and 12 dB SINAD is the usual FM sensitivity point. A software-defined radio digitizes the IF or RF so that most functions become software.

steps.prompt: Making a receiver's IF bandwidth {{k}} times wider raises its noise floor by {{10*log10(k)||2}} dB.
steps.explanation: True. Noise power $kTB$ is proportional to bandwidth: $10\log_{10}$({{k}}) = {{10*log10(k)||3}} dB more noise, so the sensitivity gets worse by the same amount. Use no more bandwidth than the signal needs.

steps.prompt: A dual-conversion receiver for {{fs|Hz|5}} has a first IF of {{if1|Hz}} (LO1 above the signal) and a second IF of 455 kHz (LO2 above the first IF).

ask.prompt: What is the LO1 frequency?
What is the LO2 frequency?
ask.explanation: The second mixer converts {{if1|Hz}} to 455 kHz with its LO above: $f_{LO2}$ = {{if1|Hz}} + 455 kHz = **{{if1+455e3|Hz|5}}**. It is a fixed crystal oscillator; tuning happens in LO1.

ask.prompt: What is the image frequency of the first conversion?
ask.explanation: $f_{im} = f_s + 2f_{IF1}$ = {{fs|Hz|5}} + {{2*if1|Hz}} = **{{fs+2*if1|Hz|5}}**, far enough away for a modest preselector. With a single 455 kHz IF the image would be only 910 kHz away.

steps.prompt: A synthesizer uses a dual-modulus {{M}}/{{M+1}} prescaler with counters $N$ = {{N}} and $A$ = {{A}}, and a {{fr|Hz}} phase-detector reference. The total division ratio is $MN + A$.

ask.prompt: What is the total division ratio?
ask.explanation: $R = MN + A$ = {{M}} × {{N}} + {{A}} = **{{M*N+A||6}}**. During each cycle the prescaler divides by {{M+1}} for $A$ counts and by {{M}} for the remaining $N - A$ counts: {{M+1}}·{{A}} + {{M}}·{{N-A}} = {{M*N+A||6}}.

ask.prompt: Find the output frequency.
To which value must $A$ change to tune {{3*fr|Hz}} higher?
ask.explanation: Each step of $A$ adds 1 to $R$ and therefore $f_{ref}$ = {{fr|Hz}} to the output. {{3*fr|Hz}} needs 3 steps: $A$ = {{A}} + 3 = **{{A+3}}** (still below $M$, so $N$ stays {{N}}).

steps.prompt: A class C PA delivers {{Po|W}} at a collector efficiency of {{100*eta|%}}, from a {{V|V}} supply. It needs {{Pd|W}} of drive power.

ask.prompt: What DC current does the PA draw?
What is its power-added efficiency PAE = $(P_{out} - P_{in})/P_{DC}$?
ask.explanation: $P_{DC}$ = {{Pdc|W}}. PAE = ({{Po|W}} − {{Pd|W}}) / {{Pdc|W}} = **{{100*(Po-Pd)/Pdc|%}}**, lower than the {{100*eta|%}} collector efficiency because the drive power is not 'free'.

steps.prompt: An L network (series L, shunt C) matches a {{Rl|Ω}} transistor output to a 50 Ω antenna at {{f|Hz}}. The transistor package adds {{Li|H}} in series with the output, and the antenna connector adds {{Cs|F}} in parallel with the load.

ask.prompt: Which inductor must be fitted?
ask.explanation: $Q = \sqrt{50/{{Rl}} - 1}$ = {{Q}}, $X_s$ = {{Q*Rl|Ω}}, so the total series inductance must be {{Q*Rl|Ω}} / (2π × {{f|Hz}}) = {{Lt|H}}. The package already provides {{Li|H}} in series: fit **{{Lt-Li|H}}**.

ask.prompt: Which capacitor must be fitted?
ask.explanation: $X_p = 50/Q$ = {{50/Q|Ω}}, so the total shunt capacitance must be 1 / (2π × {{f|Hz}} × {{50/Q|Ω}}) = {{Ct|F}}. The stray {{Cs|F}} is in parallel and adds: fit **{{Ct-Cs|F}}**.

steps.prompt: A receiver has a noise figure of {{NF2}} dB. An LNA with NF = {{NF1}} dB and a gain of {{G1}} dB is added in front of it. (Friis: $F = F_1 + (F_2 - 1)/G_1$, all as ratios.)

ask.prompt: What is the noise figure of the combination?
By how many dB does the minimum detectable signal improve?
ask.explanation: Bandwidth and required S/N are unchanged, so the sensitivity improves by the drop in noise figure: {{NF2}} − {{10*log10(Ft)||3}} = **{{NF2-10*log10(Ft)|dB}}**. The LNA's gain makes the noisy receiver behind it almost irrelevant.

steps.prompt: A receiver with {{B|Hz}} bandwidth and {{NF}} dB noise figure needs {{snr}} dB S/N. The antenna delivers {{Pr}} dBm.

ask.prompt: What is the S/N at the detector?
What is the link margin (received power minus minimum detectable signal)?
ask.explanation: MDS = noise floor + required S/N = {{Pm-snr||5}} + {{snr}} = {{Pm||5}} dBm. Margin = {{Pr}} − ({{Pm||5}}) = **{{Pr-Pm||3}} dB**: the signal may fade this much before reception fails.

steps.prompt: A receiver tuned to 100 MHz has a single preselector with $Q$ = {{q}} and high-side injection. Set the **lowest** IF that gives {{T}} dB image rejection.
steps.explanation: Need $\sqrt{1 + Q^2\rho^2} = 10^{ {{T}}/20}$, so $\rho$ = {{rho||3}}. Solving $r - 1/r = \rho$ for $r = f_{im}/f_s$ gives $r$ = {{r||4}}, $f_{im}$ = {{100*r||4}} MHz and $f_{IF} = (f_{im} - f_s)/2$ = **{{ft||3}} MHz**. A sharper preselector (higher $Q$) allows a lower IF.
